Cyanosis in the Newborn

lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • A cyanotic newborn who is working to breathe (grunting, flaring, retractions) and pinks up on oxygen has lung disease; comfortable tachypnea with no rise on 100% oxygen is a fixed right-to-left shunt.
  • A preductal saturation above postductal means right-to-left flow across the ductus: persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), or coarctation, which can give lower-extremity cyanosis from birth.
  • With a normal examination, the trigger decides: worse with feeding, better with crying is bilateral choanal atresia; worse with crying is a tetralogy of Fallot (tet) spell.

Central cyanosis shows in the lips and mucous membranes. Blue hands and feet with pink mucous membranes is acrocyanosis, common in the first hours of life and normal. Persistent pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, transient tachypnea, respiratory distress syndrome, heart anomalies and pneumothorax.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
No rise on 100% oxygen with weak pulses or falling blood pressureStart prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) and obtain echocardiography; instability raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion.
No rise on 100% oxygenStart PGE1 when cyanosis is severe or a ductal-dependent lesion such as transposition is likely; obtain echocardiography.
Preductal saturation above postductal with distress after meconiumTreat PPHN: oxygen, ventilation as needed and inhaled nitric oxide; echocardiography confirms.
Cyanosis with every feed that clears with cryingPlace an oral airway and feed by orogastric tube while the nasal passages are checked.
3Differential
Sorting by physiology
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Minutes to hours after a preterm birth: grunting, retractions, oxygen-responsive; ground-glass with air bronchograms.Start CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure); surfactant if it fails.
Soon after a term cesarean: mild distress; perihilar streaking, fluid often in the fissures; usually clears in 2 to 3 days.Give oxygen and supportive care.
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newbornTerm, after meconium or perinatal stress: preductal above postductal, poor response to oxygen, a film often clear; maternal selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) use.Obtain echocardiography; give inhaled nitric oxide.
Within hours of birth: comfortable tachypnea, no murmur, single loud S2; no rise on oxygen.Start PGE1 to keep the ductus open; echocardiography confirms.
Often from birth, with shock as the ductus closes by day 10: postductal below preductal, weak femoral pulses.Start PGE1; obtain echocardiography.
After preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, even with intrapartum penicillin; looks like respiratory distress syndrome.Obtain cultures and start antibiotics while awaiting them.
Normal examination: sorting by trigger
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Bilateral choanal atresiaFrom birth: blue at rest or with feeding, pink with crying.Pass a catheter through each naris; CT confirms.
Cyanosis worse with crying and agitation, plus a harsh murmur.Place in knee-chest position and give oxygen; obtain echocardiography.
Transposition of the great arteriesConstant cyanosis, unchanged by feeding or crying or oxygen.Start PGE1; echocardiography confirms.
Coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds.Pass an orogastric tube and obtain a radiograph.
Inspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommon.Evaluate it as noisy breathing; it does not explain cyanosis at rest.
MethemoglobinemiaCyanosis unchanged by crying or oxygen; chocolate-colored blood, normal arterial oxygen pressure (PaO2); benzocaine or nitrites in well water.Check a methemoglobin level; treat with methylene blue.
Temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding.Obtain cultures and start antibiotics.
Intraventricular hemorrhagePreterm; lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures.Obtain a head ultrasound.
4Workup

Pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours or later: positive with any reading under 90%, or, on repeat checks 1 hour apart, both hand and foot under 95% or a hand-foot gap over 3%. A positive screen calls for evaluation for heart disease, starting with echocardiography.

Redrawn rather than reproduced. Prostaglandin E1 starts when cyanosis is severe or a ductal-dependent lesion such as transposition is likely; echocardiography then names the lesion.

Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Grunting, flaring, retractionsLung disease; cyanotic heart disease gives comfortable tachypneaObtain a chest radiograph.
Saturation 65% rising to 92% on oxygenRecruitable alveoli; this excludes transpositionTreat the lung disease.
Right hand and foot both 65%No ductal gradient: against PPHN and coarctationObtain a chest radiograph.
Thirty minutes oldToo early for a ductal-dependent lesion: ductal closure typically begins within 10 to 15 hoursRepeat pulse oximetry at 24 hours or later.
One dose of antenatal glucocorticoidsLowers the risk of respiratory distress syndrome; never excludes itKeep respiratory distress syndrome on the list.

Pause point. Oxygen helps a ventilation-perfusion mismatch; a fixed shunt sends blood past the lungs, so the saturation barely moves.

Treatment by cause
CauseAction
Respiratory distress syndromeCPAP; intubation and surfactant for severe or failing cases.
Ductal-dependent heart lesionPGE1 infusion to hold the ductus open.
Persistent pulmonary hypertensionOxygen and inhaled nitric oxide.
Bilateral choanal atresiaOral airway with orogastric feeding; definitive surgical repair.
MethemoglobinemiaMethylene blue.
Practice
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; PGE1 keeps the ductus open while echocardiography confirms the lesion
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks, feeding well. Heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, afebrile. No murmur; femoral pulses 2+. Pulse oximetry: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. The same on repeat checks 1 and 2 hours later. → Echocardiography → a hand-foot gap over 3% that persists on repeat checks an hour apart fails the screen; with no other cause of hypoxemia found, echocardiography follows
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 50/min, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
  18. 2-day-old girl born at 40 weeks desaturates to 82% within moments of each breastfeed and recovers to 95% when she cries; afebrile, HR 144/min, lungs clear, no murmur; a soft catheter stops in the nasopharynx on both sides → Oral airway and orogastric feeding → Bilateral choanal atresia; confirm with CT or nasal endoscopy, then surgical repair
Decoy note Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS, so antibiotics are started empirically pending cultures. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful: in hypoplastic left heart syndrome it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and shifts right ventricular output to the lungs. · A lesion that depends on the duct presents as the duct closes, which typically begins within 10 to 15 hours. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning. · Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes. Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesion catalog once the sort points to the heart. Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the newborn clock (which diagnosis belongs at which hour) and includes choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours group. Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the step after a positive catheter test: which syndrome includes the choanal atresia, and acrocyanosis as the decoy beside a trisomy 18 murmur.
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeContinuous positive airway pressure: a respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs. The rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension: That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn) gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn: it is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta: The duct typically begins to constrict within 10 to 15 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot: its trigger is inverted. Tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink, and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia: Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia: It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon
